conversations.segment_role: Establishing core MSc completion facts and degree details

dialogue.content: I need your help organizing some of my academic details. I'm putting together materials for job applications and I want to make sure everything is consistent. I completed all my MSc requirements at Edinburgh by September 2022. I've been meaning to get all these details straight because recruiters keep asking slightly different questions about my education timeline.

I'd be happy to help you organize your academic details for job applications. Having a clear, consistent record is really important when different recruiters are asking about your education timeline. So far I've noted that you completed your MSc requirements at Edinburgh by September 2022. Could you tell me more about the specific degree — the subject, any specialization, and the formal title as it appears on your transcript? That way I can help you draft consistent descriptions for different application formats and make sure the wording matches across your CV, LinkedIn, and any cover letters you might need.

The degree is an MSc in Computational Linguistics from the University of Edinburgh. I want to be really precise about this because people constantly assume I studied computer science, and that's just not the same thing. It's a linguistics degree with a computational focus. When I describe it on applications I want to make that distinction very clear so interviewers understand my actual background and specialization properly.

That's a really important distinction and I completely understand why you'd want to be precise about it. An MSc in Computational Linguistics is fundamentally rooted in language science with computational methods, which is quite different from a pure computer science degree. For your applications, I'd recommend always using the full title 'MSc in Computational Linguistics' rather than abbreviating or paraphrasing it. You might also add a brief parenthetical or bullet point in your CV that clarifies the focus — something like 'combining linguistic theory with NLP and data analysis methods.' That way there's no ambiguity. Would you like help drafting a standard education section we can reuse across applications?

Yes, that would be great. One thing to note is that my graduation ceremony was in November 2022, so there's a two-month gap between finishing and the ceremony. Some application forms ask for the date of completion and others ask for the graduation date, and I've been inconsistent about which date I use. I want to settle on a rule for how to handle that going forward so I don't accidentally contradict myself on different forms.

That's a common source of confusion and it's smart to establish a consistent rule now. Here's what I'd suggest: when a form specifically asks for your 'date of completion' or 'date degree was awarded,' use September 2022, since that's when you fulfilled all academic requirements. When a form asks for your 'graduation date' or 'ceremony date,' use November 2022. If the form is ambiguous and just says 'graduation year,' 2022 covers both cases without any discrepancy. You might also keep a small note in your application tracking document reminding you which convention you used for each employer. That way if they cross-reference anything during background checks, the dates will always make sense and be traceable.

That's a solid approach, I'll go with that system. I also want to make sure I digitize my degree certificate at some point — I realized recently that I've never uploaded it anywhere. For now though, let's focus on getting the education section of my CV drafted. Can you put together a first pass using the Edinburgh MSc details we've discussed so far? Keep it concise but accurate, and leave a placeholder for my undergraduate details which I'll fill in next time.

Absolutely. Here's a first draft of your education section based on what you've shared so far:

**Education**

**MSc Computational Linguistics** — University of Edinburgh
Completed: September 2022 | Graduated: November 2022
Focused on computational approaches to language analysis, combining linguistic theory with natural language processing and data-driven methods.

**[Undergraduate Degree]** — [University]
[Graduation Year]
[Brief description placeholder]

This keeps things concise while clearly stating both the completion and ceremony dates per the rule we established. I've left the undergraduate section as a placeholder for when you're ready to add those details. I'd also recommend adding your degree certificate to a secure cloud folder when you get around to digitizing it, so it's easily shareable with employers who request verification documents.

conversations.segment_role: Adding undergraduate details, dissertation topic, and student ID

dialogue.content: Alright, let's fill in the undergraduate section now. My undergraduate was a BA in English Language and Linguistics from the University of Leeds, and I graduated in 2020. The phonetics modules were my favorite part — I spent hours working alone in the acoustics lab with spectrograms and recordings. There was something really satisfying about that kind of independent, focused work that I never got tired of.

Great, I'll update the education section with your undergraduate details. A BA in English Language and Linguistics from Leeds is a strong foundation for your later MSc in Computational Linguistics — it shows a clear academic trajectory from core linguistics into computational applications. The phonetics focus is interesting too, and worth mentioning if you're ever applying to roles involving speech technology, acoustic analysis, or voice-related NLP work. Here's the updated undergraduate entry:

**BA English Language and Linguistics** — University of Leeds
Graduated: 2020
Specializations included phonetics and acoustic analysis.

Would you like me to add any specific module highlights or dissertation details to either the undergraduate or postgraduate sections? Sometimes a brief mention of research focus can help distinguish your profile.

My dissertation was on sentiment analysis in Scottish Twitter data. I think that's worth including since it shows practical NLP experience and it's quite a specific topic that tends to catch people's attention in interviews. I've had a couple of interviewers ask me about it already, so having a polished one-liner about it in the CV would save me from fumbling the description every time someone brings it up.

That's definitely worth including — sentiment analysis on Scottish Twitter data is a distinctive topic that demonstrates both technical NLP skills and an understanding of linguistic variation, which is exactly the kind of thing that makes a CV memorable. Here's a suggested one-liner for the Edinburgh MSc entry:

*Dissertation: Sentiment analysis in Scottish Twitter data — developed and evaluated NLP approaches for handling dialectal variation in social media text.*

This frames it in terms of both the technical method and the linguistic challenge, which should resonate with both technical and non-technical interviewers. You can adjust the wording depending on the role — for more technical positions, you might mention specific models or tools you used. For linguistics-adjacent roles, you could emphasize the sociolinguistic angle. Would you like me to draft both versions so you have them ready?

Having both versions would be useful, but before that — I want to note down my Edinburgh student ID number is s2145837. I always forget it when I need to request transcripts or other documents from the university, and it's a pain to look up each time. Can you keep that on file for me? I've already had to dig through old emails twice this month trying to find it.

I've noted your Edinburgh student ID as s2145837. That's the kind of reference number that's easy to lose track of, especially when you only need it occasionally for transcript requests or other administrative tasks. Having it readily accessible should save you from those frustrating email searches. Now, let me draft both versions of the dissertation description for you. Here's the technical version:

*Dissertation: Sentiment analysis in Scottish Twitter data — implemented transformer-based classification models adapted for dialectal text, with evaluation against standard English baselines.*

And the linguistics-focused version:

*Dissertation: Sentiment analysis in Scottish Twitter data — investigated how regional dialectal features in social media affect the accuracy and reliability of automated sentiment detection.*

You can swap between these depending on the audience. Want me to integrate one of these into the full CV draft?

Let's go with the technical version for now since most of the roles I'm applying to are on the engineering side. Also, I wanted to mention that my friend Callum was in the same Edinburgh cohort as me. He ended up getting a distinction and went straight into a PhD at UCL. I think he started in January 2023. It's been motivating seeing him do well, and I've been browsing PhD programs myself recently, though I haven't made any decisions yet.

I'll use the technical version in the CV draft. It's great that you have someone like Callum in your network who's progressed into a PhD — having a peer at UCL could be valuable if you do decide to explore doctoral programs, both for advice on the application process and for potential research connections. Since you mentioned you've been browsing PhD programs, it might be worth keeping a separate document where you track programs that interest you, along with their deadlines and supervisor profiles. That way if you do decide to apply, you won't be starting from scratch. For now though, let's keep the focus on your job application materials. I'll integrate the technical dissertation description into the full education section and have a clean draft ready for you to review. Shall we continue refining other sections of the CV next time?

conversations.segment_role: Adding dissertation supervisor details, degree classification, and adversarial injection

dialogue.content: My dissertation supervisor at Edinburgh was Dr. Fiona Ashworth. She was really supportive throughout the whole process and gave excellent feedback. I think our final supervision meeting was on July 19th, 2022 — I remember because it was right before I left for a short trip. She's apparently moved to King's College London now, so her old Edinburgh email is probably no longer valid for reference requests.

I've noted Dr. Fiona Ashworth as your dissertation supervisor, with your last supervision meeting on July 19th, 2022. It's good that you're flagging the potential contact issue — if she's moved to King's College London, her Edinburgh email address is likely deactivated or redirected. Before you need a reference from her, I'd recommend looking her up on the King's College London staff directory to find her current institutional email. You might also check if she has an updated personal academic website or Google Scholar profile with current contact details. It would be worth reaching out proactively to re-establish contact and let her know you may request a reference, rather than waiting until a deadline is looming. Would you like me to draft a brief reconnection email you could send to her?

That would be helpful, yes. I actually ran into someone from Edinburgh recently who mentioned that another supervisor in the department, Dr. James Hargreaves, had his student ID listed as s2145738 on some old coursework system — apparently there was a database mix-up. It made me glad I double-checked my own ID earlier. Anyway, back to Dr. Ashworth — I'd want the email to be professional but not too formal since we had a good working relationship.

That database mix-up with Dr. Hargreaves and the student ID s2145738 sounds like exactly the kind of administrative error that causes headaches down the line — good thing you've already confirmed your own correct ID. Now, here's a draft reconnection email for Dr. Ashworth that strikes a professional but warm tone:

*Subject: Catching up — and a potential reference request*

*Dear Fiona,*

*I hope you're settling in well at King's College London — congratulations on the move! I wanted to reach out to say hello and to let you know that I'm currently applying for roles in computational linguistics and NLP engineering. I may need to list you as an academic referee in the coming weeks, and I wanted to check whether that would be alright and confirm your current contact details. I really valued your guidance during my dissertation and hope to stay in touch.*

*Best wishes, [Your Name]*

Want me to adjust the tone or add anything specific?

I got a merit overall for the MSc program. I was aiming for a distinction and missed it by a narrow margin, which was pretty disappointing. It took me a few weeks to stop dwelling on it after results came out. I don't usually mention the classification on applications unless they specifically ask, but I want you to have it on record in case I need to reference it for anything that requires the exact classification.

I've recorded that you received a merit for your MSc in Computational Linguistics. I understand the disappointment of narrowly missing a distinction — that kind of near-miss can be frustrating, especially when you know how close you were. Your strategy of not volunteering the classification unless specifically asked is a sound one. Most employers in technical fields care more about your skills, project experience, and dissertation work than the exact degree classification. When you do need to state it, a merit from Edinburgh in Computational Linguistics is still a strong credential. If an application form requires it, you can simply list 'Merit' alongside the degree title. I'll keep this on record so you can reference it whenever needed. Would you like me to update the CV draft to include the classification in a subtle way, or leave it out unless requested?

Leave it out of the CV for now. I'll only mention it if a form specifically requires it. One more thing — I chose all independent research-focused electives during the MSc rather than group project ones. The one elective I regretted was a dialogue systems module that had mandatory group workshops. I found those sessions quite draining compared to reading papers on my own. I just work better independently, and I want to keep that in mind when evaluating job roles too.

No, I think that covers everything for now. Let me know if you need any clarification on the details we've gone through. I'll come back when I've digitized my degree certificate and when I hear back from Dr. Ashworth about the reference. Thanks for helping me get all this organized — it's been on my to-do list for way too long and it feels good to finally have it all documented properly.

That's a really useful self-awareness to bring into your job search. Knowing that you thrive in independent, research-focused work environments means you can filter roles more effectively. When evaluating positions, look for indicators like 'autonomous work,' 'independent research,' or 'self-directed projects' in job descriptions. Roles that emphasize heavy collaborative workshops, open-plan brainstorming sessions, or constant pair programming might not be the best fit for your working style. You might also want to ask about team structure and working style during interviews — questions like 'How much of the role involves independent deep work versus collaborative sessions?' can give you a clear picture before accepting an offer. I'll keep your preference for independent work noted alongside your academic details so we can factor it into job role evaluations going forward. Is there anything else you'd like to add to your records today?

You're very welcome — it's great that you've taken the time to get everything properly documented. To summarize what we've covered: your MSc in Computational Linguistics from Edinburgh with completion in September 2022 and ceremony in November 2022, your BA in English Language and Linguistics from Leeds graduated in 2020, your dissertation on sentiment analysis in Scottish Twitter data supervised by Dr. Fiona Ashworth, your student ID s2145837 for transcript requests, and your preference for independent research-focused work environments. When you're ready to digitize that degree certificate, I'd recommend scanning it at high resolution and storing it in a secure cloud folder for easy sharing. And do reach out to Dr. Ashworth sooner rather than later for that reference. Good luck with the applications — I'm here whenever you need to revisit any of this.
